newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM's party splits, but government is safe.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM's party splits, but government is safe.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party split on Saturday but it posed no threat to his two-month-old coalition government, the leader of the breakaway group said.

Supporters of party president Laloo Prasad Yadav declared the formation of a breakaway group, which they named Rashtriya (National) Janata Dal. Yadav had led a boycott of the party's presidential election ballot on Thursday.
"I want to assure Mr Gujral that we will not allow anyone to pull the rug from under his feet. We will do and die to stay with the government," Yadav told hundreds of supporters.
The rebels of the Janata Dal, which heads India's ruling 15-party United Front coalition, passed a resolution after efforts by senior party leaders to avert a split failed.

"Keeping in mind the mandate to promote social justice and secularism and to strengthen the country's unity and integrity, this convention renames Janata Dal as the Rashtriya (National) Janata Dal," the resolution said.

Yadav, chief minister of the populous eastern state of Bihar, alleged that the voter list in the election had been rigged in favour of his leadership challenger, Sharad Yadav, no relative of his but also a fellow low-caste leader.
Results of Thursday's balloting are expected on Sunday.
The breakaway group would continue to stay in the ruling coalition, its spokesman Som Pal said, declaring: "We will remain in the government."
Yadav announced he had the backing of 18 lower house lawmakers. The breakaway group has three government ministers.
Laloo Yadav's differences are mainly with former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who Yadav's supporters say played an unfair role in an effort to dislodge their leader.

Yadav, who is seen having differences with Deve Gowda over personal ambitions and political strategy, accused the former prime minister of being soft on Hindu nationalists, a common foe against whom the parties of the ruling coalition are united.
"I don't speak against any leader but this time I will speak out against Deve Gowda," Yadav said. "He did not speak a single word against any BJP (opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party) leader."
Gujral has not publicly taken sides in the leadership battle and is believed to be neutral.
Janata Dal has 45 lawmakers in the 545-seat lower house, Lok Sabha, in which the United Front has an overall 178 members, most of whom belong to regional groups or leftist allies.

The ruling coalition's life-breath is the Congress party, India's oldest political machine, whose 140 deputies offer make-or-break support to the government in an axis formed to keep out the Hindu nationalists, who control 194 votes.
Rival parties accuse the BJP of a bias against India's minority Moslems.
Gujral became prime minister in April after the Congress forced Deve Gowda's government to fall and renewed support to the coalition on condition it changed its leader.

Laloo Yadav is also embroiled in a $280-million "fodder" scandal, in which the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has indicted him among 56 politicians and officials named in alleged embezzlement of state animal welfare funds.
Yadav says he is innocent, and alleges that the CBI is helping his political rivals. He has refused to resign as Bihar's chief minister and face trial on corruption charges.
